t: Minimum Numbers of Function Calls to Make Target Array - Thinking in Binary
o: Despite the scary setup, modify offers only two moves: increment a single element by 1, or double every element at once. Building targets bottom-up mirrors writing them in binary - each 1-bit of a value costs one private increment, while climbing to each bit level costs one global doubling shared by the whole array. Hence the answer is the total number of set bits across all values plus the largest bit length among them minus one (or simply 0 if every element is already 0). Checking the samples: [1,5] has 1 + 2 = 3 set bits and a top bit length of 3, so 3 + 2 = 5 calls; [4,2,5] has 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 set bits and again 2 doublings, totaling 6.
k: Increments are per-element and equal to the popcount of each target; doublings are global and equal to the highest bit position in use.
Running the process backwards - fix odd values, then halve everything - exposes the same greedy structure without memorizing a formula.
With nums[i] below 10^9, each element spans at most 30 bits, so the closed-form solution is one linear scan.

a.i: Replay the construction in reverse, from nums down to all zeros: undoing an increment is decrementing one element, and undoing a global double is halving everything. The greedy rule is forced by necessity - odd elements must each absorb one decrement call, and if anything remains positive the array must absorb one halving call. Counting these calls reproduces an optimal forward plan because no forward schedule can avoid fixing parities one-by-one or skip a required doubling level.
s: While any element is positive, decrement every odd element, one call each.
If some element is still positive, halve all elements and charge one call.
Repeat the two phases until every element is zero.
a.t: O(n * log C) - at most about 30 halving rounds for values up to 10^9.
a.sp: O(1) - the input array is modified in place.

a.i: Encode the binary insight directly: each element contributes popcount(x) increment calls, and the shared doubling count equals the highest set-bit index found anywhere in the array (0 when the array is all zeros). One pass accumulates both quantities using native bit intrinsics - __builtin_popcount and __builtin_clz in C++, Integer.bitCount and numberOfLeadingZeros in Java, Math.clz32 in JavaScript. No mutation and no round-by-round looping; the answer falls out of the scan.
s: Accumulate the number of set bits of every element.
Track the maximum set-bit index seen, skipping zeros to avoid undefined shifts.
Return total set bits plus the tracked maximum (which stays 0 for an all-zero array).
a.t: O(n) - constant bounded (at most 30-step) bit work per element.

w: Voice the binary reasoning first, then implement the closed form; fall back to backward simulation if the derivation stalls mid-interview - both earn full marks. Pitfalls: charging bit length instead of bit length minus one for the doublings, botching the all-zero array (answer is 0, not 1), and JavaScript sign issues - use unsigned right shifts so large values behave. Also note the answer is guaranteed to fit a 32-bit integer, so no bignum is needed despite n up to 10^5. Follow-ups: reconstruct the exact call sequence, or change the rules so doubling touches only a subrange.
